title: Adaptive TTL and access-aware archival for audit ingestion
creator: Aisha Rao
description: Problem: Our current audit ingestion pipeline applies a coarse retention policy (30/90/365) and places all indexed events in the same storage tier, which inflates index size and storage spend. Sensitive events (admin actions, SSO/SAML assertions, RBAC changes) require longer retention and higher fidelity for compliance; low-value telemetry can be aggressively compacted. Goal: implement an ingestion-side adaptive TTL and access-aware archival policy that tags events with retention metadata at ingest, routes high-sensitivity traffic to hot indexes, compacts/rolls up low-sensitivity events into summarized indices, and automatically archives cold data to object storage with fast rehydration. This ticket covers design and implementation of the ingestion enrichment, retention decision engine, partitioning adjustments, and cost-control knobs for per-tenant policies.
acceptance_criteria: Ingestion enrichment adds sensitivity_score and rbac_role_hash fields to events with <5ms per-event overhead
Retention decision engine supports YAML rules (examples) and assigns a retention_ttl to 100% of ingested events
Hot/warm/cold routing implemented: hot stays in search indices, warm gets compressed segments, cold archived to S3-compatible object store
Cold archival includes summarized rollups (time-based aggregates) and raw-event cold buckets; rollups must reduce searchable index footprint by >=50% for cold queries
Rehydration workflow (cold->warm/hot) restores archived raw events and makes them queryable within 2 hours for admin-initiated restores and <30m for automated policy lifts
Per-tenant cost controls: admins can set max_monthly_storage_gb and auto-eviction policies; enforce at ingestion time and surface quota alerts in Console
Automated simulation tool projects storage and cost impact and demonstrates >=35% cost reduction on sample workload within staging
End-to-end integration tests and benchmark results committed, plus docs updated in Confluence and Console UI spec finalized
Security review completed and signoff obtained for RBAC/SAML enrichment and storage access patterns
tasks: Design: define sensitivity heuristics and YAML rule schema
Proto: implement enrichment library in ingestion consumer (Go) that computes sensitivity_score and rbac_role_hash
Policy engine: implement retention rule evaluator as sidecar with unit tests
Routing: add topic-level partitioning by sensitivity and customer to Kafka; update streamer to select appropriate index/codec
Storage: implement cold archive writer that writes raw+metadata to object store with index of manifests
Rollups: create daily/hourly rollup job to generate summarized indices for cold tier
Rehydration: implement restore job and test runbooks for manual and automatic restores
Console: add per-tenant storage cap controls and alerts UI mockups
Metrics & dashboards: storage spend by tenant, retention compliance, rehydrate latency, index size per shard
Documentation: Confluence design doc, runbooks, and Console help text
Security review and encryption KMS integration
notes: Decision: keep sensitivity scoring deterministic and explainable (no opaque ML scoring in first iteration). Use weighted rule list: admin_action +10, sso_assertion +8, rbac_change +12, failed_login +3, data_export +15
Trade-off: Storing raw events in cold object store keeps fidelity but increases archive costs; rollups will cover most query needs and raw restores reserved for compliance/legal ops
Performance estimate: adding enrichment ~0.5-4ms per event depending on lookups; batching and local caches will reduce p50 to ~0.8ms in benchmark
Partition plan: keep daily time-based partitions for hot index, append sensitivity shard to partition key to reduce cross-shard queries for high-sensitivity reads

Cost modelling: simulated sample tenant (50M events/month) -> current monthly storage 4TB, projected after rollups and archive: 1.6TB (60% savings); additional object store egress expected for restores estimated at 120GB/month
API: retention rules as YAML will live in Git-backed configs per-organization; Console will expose editable rule preview with estimated cost impact
Data classification: integrate with RBAC v2 to mark service-accounts vs human admins so policy can extend retention for human admin actions only
SAML enrichment: capture assertion_id, issuer, and authn_context to aid investigations; ensure PII minimization—strip raw SAML payloads unless flagged by policy
